rummeln.et: From Middle High German rummeln, ultimately onomatopoeic, similar to Dutch rommelen.

rumoren.et: Middle High German rumōren, from Latin rumōr.

rumsen.et: rums + -en, the first element being an onomatopoeia used to describe the impact of something dropping.

rümpfen.et: From Middle High German rümpfen, from Old High German (h)rimpfan, from Proto-West Germanic *hrimpan, from Proto-Germanic *hrimpaną (“to wrinkle”).

s: initial and final clipping (e.g. Elisabeth → Lisa)

Rumtürkisch.et: Coined by Austrian orientalist Paul Wittek in 1939, calque of Ottoman Turkish لسان ترك رومی (lisan-ı Türk-i Rumi, literally “language of the Turks of Anatolia”).

s: to make a low-pitched thudding or tumbling sound (often with a degree of irregularity)
to rumble (to move with a heavy, low-pitched sound)

It happened in a small town not far from La Junta in Colorado. In the beautiful summer morning, the freight train rumbled onwards, now stopping, then rumbling back and forth again. And then there was quiet.
rumpeln.et: From Middle High German rumpeln, from Middle Low German rumpelen, ultimately onomatopoeic iteratives.

Rumpelfußball.et: From rumpeln (“to rumble, trundle”) + Fußball (“football”). Coined by Franz Beckenbauer in 2000.

rumoxidieren.et: From rum- + oxidieren. Initially popularized by the comedy Werner – Beinhart! in the first sense (see quote), where it refers to an actual metal part at risk of rusting, though this was quickly generalized. In 2015 it gained further notoriety, coming third in …

s: to make out, to French-kiss etc.
Hattest du was mit dem? – Naja, wir haben nur rumgemacht.

rummachen.et: By surface analysis, rum- (“around”) + machen (“to do, make”).

s: to act lovey-dovey, to fool around
to be able to avoid/get around something

all the same; either way; it makes no difference; used to indicate that the given options are practically equivalent without a strong preference for either
Ob du rechts oder links anfängst, ist rum wie num.
Whether you start from the right or from the left doesn't matter at all.
Vielleicht ist hier an Ellipse zu denken; denn eher versteht man jedenfalls solche komparativen Wendungen, als da sind „Wurst wie Suppe“, „Jacke wie Hose“, „’rum wie ’num.“

Maybe ellipsis is to be considered here; for such comparative phrasings would definitely be more likely to be understood, such as "sausage like soup", "jacket like pants", "this way around like that way around".
